concept.name: Reverse iron condor
concept.definition: A reverse iron condor (long iron condor) is a four-leg, same-expiration strategy combining a bear put spread (long higher put, short lower put) and a bull call spread (long lower call, short higher call) — the mirror image of the standard iron condor, entered for a net debit. It profits when the underlying moves beyond either of the long inner strikes, with both maximum gain and loss fixed.
concept.intuition: It is a long strangle with the far tails sold off: you pay a smaller debit for a big-move bet, accepting a capped payoff instead of unlimited upside.
concept.mechanics: Net debit = premium paid minus premium received; maximum loss is the debit if the underlying finishes between the long inner strikes; maximum gain is the wing width minus the debit beyond either outer (short) strike. It is long volatility and long gamma between the inner strikes.
concept.formula: Max loss = net debit; max gain = wing width - net debit; breakevens = long put strike - debit and long call strike + debit.
concept.failure_modes: The most likely outcome is losing the full debit, since the underlying must travel past the inner strikes before any payoff accrues; post-event implied-volatility collapses erode the position even when the directional view is right.
concept.misconceptions: It is not 'an iron condor with unlimited profit' — the outer short strikes cap the payoff, which is precisely what makes it a debit trade cheaper than a strangle.
concept.example: With XYZ at $100: sell $90 put, buy $95 put, buy $105 call, sell $110 call for a $2.00 net debit. Max loss $200 between $95 and $105; max gain $300 at or beyond $90 or $110.
